A well foundation is typically 4–8 m long and 0.8–3.0 m in diameter; it is competitive with piles if the bearing stratum is not too deep, especially with high groundwater, when the foundation level has to be taken below the water table.

In soft clay, peat, flowing (submerged) sand and with a very high groundwater table, the slurry can hardly support the wall of the trench – in such cases the diaphragm wall reaches its limits.

Which statement is true of large-diameter piles (above 80 cm)?

The strip footing of the old masonry wall is overloaded: the pressure under the footing on the soft layer is high, the wall has settled and cracked – or storeys are to be added, which would bring even more load. The bearing stratum lies deeper.
A steel core is placed in the bore (or the hollow drill rod stays in), and the grout is injected from the bottom up. In the bearing stratum the cement body and the permeated, rough sleeve form.

The upper part of the pile is bonded to the old structure by grouting within the existing footing (with a new reinforced concrete capping beam if needed). It is often preloaded with a jack so that the load is transferred immediately.

The micropiles transfer the load of the wall to the bearing stratum along their shafts – no base resistance is assumed. The pressure under the old footing decreases and the settlement stops; the basement can even be deepened.

What is the maximum shaft diameter of a bored micropile?
The shaft diameter of a bored micropile is at most 250–300 mm; the 150 mm limit applies to the largest cross-sectional dimension of a driven micropile.

The wall of an old apartment block stands on an overloaded, cracked strip footing. Step through how the micropiles take over the load – drilled from the cellar and from outside, without demolishing the house.

Section: old wall with a strip footing, cellar, soft layer and a deeper bearing stratum; the micropiles are drilled alternately from the cellar and from outside, obliquely through the footing, and cross each other

Illustrative figure, with distorted scale: in reality the micropiles are typically 6–15 m long, closely spaced along the wall, drilled alternately from the cellar and from outside with crossing inclinations. How the load is shared between the footing and the piles depends on the preloading and on further settlement.

The small drilling rig fits into the cellar: from there they drill obliquely down through the existing footing to the bearing stratum. The next pile is drilled from outside, from ground level, with the opposite inclination, also through the footing. The piles thus cross each other, and are installed alternately along the wall, offset from one another. No driving, no vibration – the house can remain occupied.
